chapter_theme: Wealth that does no good (நன்றியில் செல்வம்): the riches of the base and ungiving are of no use to anyone near them, and the poor turn away to givers however far. The chapter also faces the scandal that wealth goes to the senseless while the good are poor, and explains it by former deeds.
structure_note: Three nature similes show that the base man's wealth draws no one (261-263). Then the chapter turns to the injustice of fortune (264-268), answered by former deeds (265) and met with a curse on Lakshmi (266), and ends on the folly of the rich man's giving (269) and a set of reversals that redefine learned, unlearned, rich and poor (270).

261.reading: Bats do not go to the wood-apple tree with its cracked trunk, though it stands near and bears much fruit; so the wealth of men without worth, however close they live, is not something anyone thinks of counting on.
261.nuance: Nearness is the point: what is close but unapproachable is as good as far. Mudaliar specifies who does not count on it: the poor.

262.reading: No one reaches for the cactus, though its small buds look lovely enough to gather by the handful, because they are not flowers to wear; so the wise do not seek out the base, however rich.
262.nuance: The cactus buds are attractive but unusable; wealth is the attraction, character the use. Shanmuganar's commentary on this quatrain appears under 261.

263.reading: Though they live on the shore of the wave-filled sea, people go and drink at a well with a strong, sweet spring; so though the rich are near, desire turns to the givers, even far away.
263.nuance: The sea is huge and useless to drink; the small well gives. Size of wealth does not draw anyone, only its being given. Mudaliar's commentary is missing for this quatrain, and Shanmuganar's appears under 261.

264.reading: In this sea-girt world merit is a thing apart: while men of understanding are there, even those with no understanding, like the dice-piece and the brinjal, live clad in silk and fine cloth.
264.nuance: புண்ணியம் (merit) is set apart from understanding: prosperity follows merit, not sense. Mudaliar works out the two images: the dice-piece that returns to the board after being cut down (the shameless who come back to the assembly) and the brinjal that fruits hidden (those who hide their wealth). Shanmuganar's commentary is missing.

265.reading: Long-eyed one, when the good and just remain poor, the only cause you will find on reflection for the unjust and unlearned having wealth is the fruit of old deeds.
265.nuance: The verse answers the scandal of undeserved wealth with former deeds, and so denies that present wealth says anything about present worth. Mudaliar specifies good deeds of a former birth. Shanmuganar's commentary is missing.

266.reading: Golden lady seated on the fine flower like its scentless outer petal, may you die and turn to ash on the earth: you leave the good, who are like gold, and go to the side of worthless men.
266.nuance: A curse on Lakshmi herself. Mudaliar explains the simile: as the outer petal lacks the flower's scent, the goddess who lives on the lotus has none of its softness.

267.reading: Does poverty feel no shame in staying with the good? Is the wealth of the useless a glue that holds fast? See with wonder, dart-eyed one, how these two stay just where they ought not.
267.nuance: Poverty and wealth are made into agents with manners: one shameless, the other sticky. The verse states the wonder without explaining it; 265 gives the explanation.

268.reading: Those who are not shameless walk long roads and live on mixed scraps, while the shameless never stir a foot and feast at home on fried dishes as rivers of ghee and milk flow over them.
268.nuance: Shame is what keeps the decent poor; its absence is what lets the others thrive. Mudaliar takes the scraps as begged food and the feasters as eating alone behind closed doors without giving; Shanmuganar names the feasters' fault as dishonesty and deceit.

269.reading: While the golden red paddy withers in the ear, the lightning-lit cloud pours its rain into the sea; the giving of fools who come into great wealth is of the same kind.
269.nuance: The fault is not that fools never give but that they give where it is not needed. Mudaliar's 'also' (உம்மை) implies they otherwise do nothing good with wealth either.

270.reading: Those without understanding remain unlearned though they study, and those with understanding are as the learned though they have not studied; those who never beg are rich though poor, and the rich are poor if they do not give.
270.nuance: Four reversals that make the inner quality, not the outward possession, decide the name. Mudaliar takes தூய்தாக as a pure mind, a condition on the poor who do not beg.

links.note: Both picture the ungiving man's wealth as a fruiting tree no one can use: a poison tree in the middle of town (Kural), a wood-apple near at hand that the bats ignore (here). Parimelazhagar also stresses that the man is near the poor.
Both picture wealth as drinking water. The Kural's wise man's wealth is the full village tank; here the rich man is the undrinkable sea and the giver the small sweet well.
Both say that being rich and being wise are separate fortunes. 264 makes the sharper point that the senseless live in silk while the wise are passed over.
Kural 169 says the prosperity of the crooked and the ruin of the upright are to be pondered. 265 gives the answer such pondering reaches: the fruit of old deeds, and nothing else.
Both invite wonder at poverty staying with the good and wealth with the unworthy. Neither verse explains it; Parimelazhagar and 265 explain it by past deeds.

Kural 179 says Fortune knows the way and goes to the wise who understand virtue; 266 says she leaves the good and goes to the worthless. Both speak of the goddess choosing whom to join. The tension holds if 179 is a claim about how fortune actually goes, as Parimelazhagar takes it, and not only a promise.
Both say study does not make one learned without understanding: the Kural names that understanding as living in accord with the world.

Both set the sea against a small well. In 263 people seek out the sweet well as they seek out givers; in 275 they wait at a nearly dry well, as the poverty of the worthy is better than wealth that forgets the next world.

source_issues: Quatrain 261: Shanmuganar's field also holds the texts and commentary of 262 and 263, and the text of 264 without commentary; Shanmuganar's commentary on 264 and 265 is missing.
Quatrain 263: Mudaliar's commentary is not aligned.
Quatrain 266: the verse reads நாறாக் தகடேபோல், apparently for நாறாத் தகடேபோல்; Mudaliar glosses நாறா.
Quatrain 270: Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of the next chapter.
